level1.text: A horizontal net force of $6.0\,\text{N}$ acts on a toy car of mass $2.5\,\text{kg}$. What is the acceleration of the toy car?
A cyclist and a bicycle with a total mass of $80\,\text{kg}$ accelerate on a horizontal road with an acceleration of $1.5\,\text{m/s}^2$. What is the net force acting on them?
A net force of $45\,\text{N}$ acts on an object, and its acceleration is $3.0\,\text{m/s}^2$. What is the mass of the object?

A box of mass $12\,\text{kg}$ is pulled on a horizontal floor with a horizontal force of $38\,\text{N}$. The friction force from the floor on the box is $20\,\text{N}$. Draw the free-body diagram of the box. What is the acceleration of the box?
At a building site a bucket of mass $8.0\,\text{kg}$ is lifted straight up on a rope at constant velocity. Draw the free-body diagram of the bucket. What is the tension in the rope?
An elevator moves upward and slows down to stop. The positive direction is up. Which statement about the net force $\Sigma\overline{F}$ acting on the elevator is correct?
level1.answer: The net force points down, because the speed decreases and the acceleration points downward.

choices.text: The net force points up, because the elevator is moving upward and the velocity determines the direction of the force.
choices.feedback: The direction of the net force is determined by the direction of the acceleration, not the velocity. When the elevator slows down, the speed decreases, so the acceleration and the net force point opposite to the velocity, that is, down.

choices.text: The net force is zero, because the direction of motion of the elevator stays upward all the time.
choices.feedback: The net force is zero only when the velocity does not change. The speed of the elevator decreases, so the acceleration is not zero. The direction of motion staying the same tells nothing about the acceleration.

choices.text: The net force points down, because the speed decreases and the acceleration points downward.
choices.feedback: Correct: by Newton's second law $\Sigma\overline{F} = m\overline{a}$, so the net force points in the direction of the acceleration. While slowing down, the elevator has a downward acceleration even though it is still moving upward. The force of the rope is then smaller than the weight.

choices.text: The net force points up, because the force of the rope is always greater than the weight when the elevator rises.
choices.feedback: The force of the rope is greater than the weight only when the rise begins. In a steady rise the forces are equal, and while slowing down the force of the rope is smaller than the weight. The net force follows the acceleration, not the direction of motion.

level1.text: The mass of an ice hockey puck is $170\,\text{g}$. A hit from the stick gives the puck a horizontal acceleration of $400\,\text{m/s}^2$. What is the net force acting on the puck during the hit?
A horizontal net force of $0.60\,\text{kN}$ acts on a snowmobile, and its acceleration is $1.5\,\text{m/s}^2$. What is the mass of the snowmobile?

A spacecraft of mass $15\,000\,\text{kg}$ landing on the Moon slows its descent with a rocket-engine thrust that points upward. The spacecraft's acceleration is $0.50\,\text{m/s}^2$ upward. Besides its weight, only the thrust acts on it. Look up the free-fall acceleration on the surface of the Moon in the MAFY table (mafytaulukot.fi). How large is the thrust?
hints: The value is found in the MAFY table under *Aurinkokunta* (the Solar System).

level1.text: The graph shows the acceleration of two carts A and B against the net force. The masses of the carts are not given. What is the mass of cart A?

level2.text: A passenger car of mass $1200\,\text{kg}$ accelerates uniformly on a horizontal road from rest to a velocity of $90\,\text{km/h}$ in $10\,\text{s}$. What is the net force acting on the car during the acceleration?

An elevator car with its passengers has a mass of $900\,\text{kg}$. It starts to move downward with an acceleration of $1.5\,\text{m/s}^2$. What is the tension in the supporting rope during the acceleration?

A crane lowers a load of $120\,\text{kg}$ downward at a velocity of $2.0\,\text{m/s}$. Just before the ground the load slows down uniformly and stops in $2.0\,\text{s}$. What is the tension in the rope during the slowing down?

Two children pull a cart of $30\,\text{kg}$ in a horizontal yard with horizontal ropes in opposite directions. One pulls with a force of $60\,\text{N}$ and the other with a force of $45\,\text{N}$. Friction is ignored. What is the acceleration of the cart?

On an air track a cart was pulled by a constant horizontal force, and the magnitude of the force was varied. The mass of the cart stayed the same, and the friction was so small that it can be ignored. For each force $F$ the acceleration $a$ of the cart was measured. The table is an example data set.

Draw the $(F, a)$ graph of the measurement points and fit a straight line through the origin to the points. Determine the slope of the line and use it to find the mass of the cart. Enter the mass of the cart in the answer box.

level2.text:
A cart was pulled on a horizontal track every time with the same horizontal force. The mass $m$ of the cart was changed by adding weights to it, and with each mass the acceleration $a$ was measured. Friction was small and is ignored. The table is an example data set.

a) For each mass calculate the reciprocal $1/m$ and draw the $(1/m, a)$ graph. Fit a straight line through the origin to the points and determine its slope. What does the slope tell you?

b) Which quantities had to be kept constant for the measurement to be a fair test? Enter the magnitude of the pulling force in the answer box.

data.caption: Acceleration of the cart with different masses (example data)

level2.text:
A crane lowers a concrete element of mass $820\,\text{kg}$ onto a quay. The element moves downward and slows down uniformly, and the magnitude of its acceleration is $1.20\,\text{m/s}^2$. Air resistance is ignored.

A student calculated the tension in the rope like this: “The element moves downward, so the acceleration points down. Thus $mg - T = ma$, from which $T = m(g - a) = 820\,\text{kg}\cdot(9.81\,\text{m/s}^2 - 1.20\,\text{m/s}^2) = 7.06\,\text{kN}$.”

What is the error in the student's solution? Calculate the correct tension in the rope. Enter the magnitude of the tension in the rope in the answer box.

A shopping trolley whose mass with its goods is $18\,\text{kg}$ is pushed on a horizontal floor with a horizontal force of $45\,\text{N}$. The friction force of the floor on the trolley is $9.0\,\text{N}$, and air resistance is neglected. A student calculates the acceleration of the trolley.

Line 1: the positive direction is the direction of the pushing force, so $\Sigma F = F - F_\mu$.

Line 2: $\Sigma F = 45\,\text{N} - 9.0\,\text{N}$, that is $\Sigma F = 36\,\text{N}$.

Line 3: $G = mg = 18\,\text{kg} \cdot 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$, that is $G \approx 177\,\text{N}$.

Line 4: $a = \dfrac{\Sigma F}{G}$, that is $a = \dfrac{36\,\text{N}}{177\,\text{N}} \approx 0.20\,\text{m/s}^2$.

Check the calculation line by line. Choose the incorrect line, or the last option if the calculation has no error.

choices.text: Line 1: expression for the net force
choices.feedback: Line 1 is correct: friction opposes the motion, so it points against the pushing force and gets a minus sign. Thinking that the line is wrong means thinking that all the forces acting on the object are added together with the same sign.

Line 2 is correct: $45\,\text{N} - 9.0\,\text{N} = 36\,\text{N}$. Thinking that the line is wrong means thinking that the acceleration is determined by the pushing force $45\,\text{N}$ alone, although it is determined by the sum of all the forces.

Line 3 is calculated correctly: $18\,\text{kg} \cdot 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2 \approx 177\,\text{N}$. The weight does not affect the horizontal motion, but calculating it is not an error. Check the other lines in the same way.

Correct, this line is wrong: the acceleration is the net force divided by the mass, not by the weight. The correct calculation is $a = 36\,\text{N} : 18\,\text{kg}$, that is $a = 2.0\,\text{m/s}^2$. The units reveal the error: $\text{N} : \text{N}$ does not give the unit $\text{m/s}^2$.

choices.text: There is no error in the calculation
choices.feedback: There is an error on line 4: the weight $G$ has been used in place of the mass $m$. On a horizontal floor the normal force cancels the weight, and the acceleration is reduced by the mass, not by the weight.

level2.text: The graph shows the acceleration of two carts A and B against the net force. The masses of the carts are not given. A horizontal net force of $2.4\,\text{N}$ acts on cart B. What is the acceleration of cart B?

level3.text: A student of mass $60.0\,\text{kg}$ stands on a bathroom scale in an elevator. The scale measures the force with which it supports the student and shows it in kilograms, that is, divides the force by $9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$. When the elevator starts to move, the scale shows $54.0\,\text{kg}$ for a moment. What is the acceleration of the elevator, and in which direction does it point?

An empty timber truck of mass $10\,\text{t}$ accelerates uniformly from rest to a velocity of $36\,\text{km/h}$ in $8.0\,\text{s}$. Fully loaded, its mass is $25\,\text{t}$. Assume that the net force during the acceleration is the same as for the empty truck. How long does it take the loaded truck to accelerate from rest to $36\,\text{km/h}$?

A child slides on a sled on horizontal snow. The total mass of the sled and the child is $30\,\text{kg}$, and the velocity is $4.0\,\text{m/s}$ at the start. Nobody pulls or pushes the sled. The friction force from the snow is $18\,\text{N}$, and air resistance is not taken into account. How long does it take before the sled stops?

Students investigate how the acceleration $a$ of a cart pulled along a table depends on the horizontal pulling force $F$. The mass of the cart stayed the same. A constant friction force from the surface acts on the moving cart. The table is an example data set.

a) Draw the $(F, a)$ graph of the measurement points and fit a straight line to the points. Justify why the line does not pass through the origin.

b) Determine the mass of the cart from the slope of the line.

c) Determine the magnitude of the friction force from the point where the line crosses the $F$-axis. Enter the magnitude of the friction force in the answer box.

level3.text:
A person of mass $70\,\text{kg}$ stands in an elevator. The elevator starts upward from rest and moves in three phases. The accelerations of phases 1 and 2 have been measured with an acceleration sensor (example data), and the positive direction is up.

In phase 3 the elevator slows down uniformly and stops at the moment $t = 13.0\,\text{s}$.

a) Calculate the greatest velocity of the elevator.

b) Calculate the acceleration of the elevator in phase 3.

c) Draw the free-body diagram of the person in phase 3 and calculate the normal force from the floor on the person. Compare it with the weight of the person and justify why the normal force differs from the weight. Enter the normal force of part c) in the answer box.

data.caption: Acceleration of the elevator in phases 1 and 2 (example data)
